questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a formal region
questions.stem: A clinician's note records that a patient lives inside a district with a fixed boundary, a named authority, and a published population count. Which type of region does this describe?

options.text: A functional region, because it is defined by the services and workplaces it contains
options.misconception: labels a rule-bound district by its service links instead

options.text: A formal region, because it is defined by a stated rule or boundary rather than by how people live
A vernacular region, because residents describe the district by the name people give it locally
options.misconception: confuses an official boundary with a name people use for a place

options.text: A site, because the district is a single fixed point that all services cluster around
options.misconception: treats an administrative area as though it were a location

questions.explanation: A formal region is drawn by a stated rule, such as an administrative boundary, and does not change with daily life. Functional regions depend on flows, and vernacular regions on shared local names.
questions.hint: Ask whether a rule or a human behaviour defines it.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a functional region
questions.stem: A clinic's catchment panel covers a town and the rural villages around it, because patients travel in from the villages for treatment. What kind of region is this catchment?

options.text: A formal region, because the health authority drew it on a map with a fixed boundary
options.misconception: relies on a drawn boundary rather than on how the area works

options.text: A vernacular region, because patients call the whole area the town and its surrounds
options.misconception: uses residents' names for the area rather than the service it provides

options.text: A site, because the hospital building is the focus that draws the whole area in
options.misconception: confuses the region with the single facility at its centre

options.text: A functional region, because it is defined by the movement of patients to a shared service

questions.explanation: A functional region is held together by the movement of people or goods towards a common activity, and its boundary changes with the flow. A drawn boundary or a local nickname does not make it functional.
questions.hint: Ask what activity ties the area together.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what vernacular regions are
questions.stem: A clinic's intake note records that patients from the same town describe their home area differently, one calling it the valley, another the old market town, and a third the district. Explain what these names reveal about vernacular regions and why they matter for a service that has to plan where to put a clinic.

answer.exemplar: Vernacular regions exist because people name the places they live by what those places mean to them, not by any rule from outside. The three names in this note cover overlapping ground and carry different emphases, one physical, one historical, one administrative, which shows that the region in people's minds is fuzzy and personal. A clinic planner who treats one label as the settled truth may place a facility where patients do not think they belong, and may miss the villages that share a name but sit outside a mapped boundary.

questions.explanation: Vernacular regions are informal and often overlapping, defined by how residents describe their home area. Since no official map matches them, a planner must test local usage rather than assume one label fits a population.
questions.hint: Ask what residents themselves call the place.

questions.learningObjective: Measure relative distance from a site
questions.stem: A relocation note records that a new health centre sits 14 kilometres from the nearest bus interchange and 3 kilometres from the village it primarily serves. How many kilometres nearer to the village is the centre than to the interchange?
questions.explanation: The difference is 14 less 3, which is 11 kilometres, so the centre is more accessible from the village. Such distances describe site, the exact spot chosen, rather than situation, the wider setting.
questions.hint: Subtract one distance from the other.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish situation from site

stimulus.body: A note on a new outpatient centre records that it stands on a former market site, is two kilometres from the old town, sits on the main bus route, and lies at the meeting point of the river road and the hill lane. The note adds that the land was cheap because flood water reached it most winters.

questions.stem: Using the note, which set of facts describes the situation rather than the site of the centre?

options.text: The centre stands on the former market site, which is the exact spot it occupies
options.misconception: lists the exact spot as though it described the wider setting

options.text: The centre lies two kilometres from the old town and on the main bus route
options.misconception: lists situational facts as though they described the exact spot

options.text: The centre's position relative to the bus route, the old town, and the flood-prone land
The centre is two kilometres from the old town, because distance alone describes the setting
options.misconception: confuses a single relative position with the whole of the setting

questions.explanation: Site is the exact spot a place occupies, while situation describes its position relative to other features and influences. The bus route, old town, and flood risk are all relational facts.
questions.hint: Ask whether the fact is a location or a relationship.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Distance at which two bid-rent curves meet
questions.learningObjective: Describe how bid-rent curves behave
questions.stem: A clinic's capital plan compares two possible uses for one plot: a specialist practice that values high street access, and a warehouse that values cheap land near the ring road. First describe how the two curves behave, then choose the distance at which the choice changes.

options.text: Both curves fall with distance, so one crossing point marks where the warehouse wins on rent
The curves rise with distance, so there is no crossing point and the warehouse always wins
options.misconception: believes willingness to pay rises with distance from the centre

options.text: The curves are flat, so the choice never changes and the practice always wins
options.misconception: assumes the rent offered is the same at every distance

options.text: The curves cross many times, so the choice changes at every crossroads on the route
options.misconception: believes two smooth curves must intersect repeatedly

questions.explanation: Bid-rent curves slope downward because location value falls with distance from the centre, and two such curves cross once. Beyond that crossing the lower-rent, land-hungry use wins.
questions.hint: Ask how the rent offered changes with distance.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why outlets space themselves out
questions.stem: A community pharmacy note records that branches appear in a region at fairly regular intervals rather than everywhere. Why do outlets of the same kind settle at intervals?

options.text: Because planners require a minimum distance between branches, so the pattern is imposed by law
options.misconception: credits regulation rather than market demand for the spacing

options.text: Because every firm must serve a fixed minimum number of patients before it can open at all
options.misconception: assumes a fixed minimum size of population before opening

options.text: Because customers travel only a short distance, so no branch ever serves more than a small area
options.misconception: assumes customers never travel far enough to reach a further branch

options.text: Because each outlet needs a threshold population nearby, and nearby outlets compete for the same trade

questions.explanation: An outlet needs enough customers within travelling distance to trade, but two close together split the same demand. Intervals emerge from threshold demand against maximum range, not from law.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when two outlets sit close together.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Classify regions by how they are defined
questions.stem: A health board's map shows three regions drawn by rule: one by parish boundary, one by distance from the nearest hospital, and one by the same soil type. Which classification does each belong to?

options.text: All three are formal, because each was drawn on a map before any patients were counted
options.misconception: treats every mapped boundary as formal

options.text: Parish and soil regions are formal, while the hospital catchment is functional
All three are functional, because each one records the movement of people towards services
options.misconception: classifies every region by the presence of movement

options.text: Parish and soil regions are functional, while the hospital catchment is formal
options.misconception: reverses which regions depend on rules and which on movement

questions.explanation: A formal region is defined by a rule that applies to any place, whether a parish or a soil type. The hospital catchment is functional because it exists only through patients travelling to a service.
questions.hint: Ask whether the boundary comes from a rule or from movement.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a functional region has a vague edge
questions.stem: A clinic's note describes a pharmacy chain whose branches draw customers from overlapping areas, so no single branch serves a clean district. Explain why this chain forms a functional region and why its boundary is hard to draw.

answer.exemplar: The chain's branches hold together an area through the flow of customers towards a shared service, which is the test for a functional region. Its boundary is hard to draw because the customers of one branch overlap heavily with those of the next, and the flow shifts with opening hours, transport links, and where a new branch opens. A formal boundary would therefore impose a tidiness the underlying behaviour does not have.

questions.explanation: A functional region is created by movement towards a service rather than a drawn line, so it exists while customers keep travelling in. Overlapping catchments and shifting travel make its edge uncertain.
questions.hint: Ask what connects the branches.

questions.stem: A clinic's intake survey finds that three in every ten patients use a local or vernacular name for their home area rather than the official district name. Among the 450 patients surveyed, how many use a vernacular name?
questions.explanation: Three in ten of 450 is 135 patients, which is the number whose naming follows local usage rather than the official map. A count of official districts would have missed every one of those informal names.
questions.hint: Multiply the fraction by the number surveyed.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Define site in relation to situation

stimulus.body: A planning note describes three possible sites for a community pharmacy. Site One stands on the main street in the town centre. Site Two is on a residential road two kilometres out with free parking. Site Three is beside the bus interchange, where footfall is highest but rents are also highest.

questions.stem: Using the planning note, which statement describes site correctly?

options.text: Site is the exact position a facility occupies, so each of the three plots has a different site of its own
Site is the wider area a facility serves, so the town centre is the site of Site One
options.misconception: defines site as the area served rather than the position occupied

options.text: Site is the set of conditions around a plot, so the bus interchange sets the site of Site Three
options.misconception: defines site as surrounding conditions rather than a position

options.text: Site is decided by which option serves most patients, so the best plot becomes the site
options.misconception: treats site as a choice outcome rather than a physical position

questions.explanation: Site names the exact spot a place occupies, given as a coordinate or plot, while situation describes the wider setting. Choosing the best plot does not make the site anything but a position.
questions.hint: Ask what a coordinate would pin down.

questions.learningObjective: Separate site from situation in a note
questions.stem: A clinician's note records a rural dispensary that serves people from a scattered settlement, three hours from the nearest hospital. First distinguish the two kinds of position, then choose the correct reading.

options.text: The settlement's site is where it stands on the map, and its situation is the number of households it contains
options.misconception: treats a local characteristic as the wider setting

options.text: The settlement's site is its distance from the hospital, and its situation is where it stands on the map
options.misconception: swaps a distance relationship with a physical position

options.text: The settlement's site is where it stands on the map, and its situation includes its isolation from the hospital
The settlement's site is its isolation from the hospital, and its situation is where it stands on the map
options.misconception: confuses the wider setting with the exact spot occupied

questions.explanation: Site is the exact position, and situation describes the influences reaching it, such as isolation from a hospital. The two are different kinds of statement about the same place.
questions.hint: Ask whether the fact is a position or a relationship.

questions.topic: Distance at which two bid-rent curves meet
questions.learningObjective: Explain the meaning of a bid-rent crossing
questions.stem: A clinician's note plans a small health centre on a plot and compares it with a competing pharmacy on an adjacent plot. What does the distance at which two bid-rent curves meet represent?

options.text: The point at which both activities become equally profitable and the rent is at its lowest
options.misconception: confuses the crossing with the point of least rent

options.text: The point at which one activity can no longer afford the land at all and must close
options.misconception: confuses the crossing with the point of commercial closure

options.text: The point at which one use can outbid the other for the same plot, so the choice changes
The point at which the two activities share the customers equally well
options.misconception: confuses outbidding land with splitting a customer base

questions.explanation: Each curve shows the maximum rent one use will pay at each distance, and where they cross one use can outbid the other. The site then changes hands, which is why the crossing matters.
questions.hint: Ask which use can pay more rent at that point.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the spacing of outlets in a region
questions.stem: A region has a population of 180,000 spread evenly, and pharmacy chains open branches roughly 12 kilometres apart. What explains the regular spacing of those branches?

options.text: Each branch needs a threshold of customers within reach, and one 12 kilometres off draws on a different pool
The spacing is set by the road network, because chains always open at the junction of two routes
options.misconception: attributes the pattern to the road network rather than to demand

options.text: The spacing is a legal requirement, because councils limit how close two pharmacies may stand
options.misconception: attributes the pattern to regulation rather than to demand

options.text: The spacing is arbitrary, because chains place branches wherever a building becomes available
options.misconception: denies any systematic pattern in branch placement

questions.explanation: Spacing reflects the balance between the population a branch needs and how far customers will travel, so a branch 12 kilometres off draws on a separate pool. Demand explains the repetition.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the two branches' customers.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Contrast formal and functional regions
questions.stem: A health board's note explains that it reports on two regions: one drawn around a single hospital catchment and one drawn around a shared geological feature. Explain why these are different kinds of region and why the distinction matters for reporting.

answer.exemplar: The hospital catchment is a functional region because it exists through the movement of patients towards a service, and its edge shifts as travel patterns change. The geological region is formal because it is defined by a physical rule that can be applied on a map to any place, and it stays put regardless of who uses it. The distinction matters because a functional region can lose or gain population without its area changing, while a formal region's population changes for reasons that have nothing to do with the boundary.

questions.explanation: A functional region is defined by movement towards an activity, while a formal region is fixed by a stated rule such as a physical feature. Reporting mixes them by presenting a fixed area as a fixed population.
questions.hint: Ask whether the population or the area is what is fixed.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of households in a functional region
questions.stem: A clinic's functional region for community nursing covers 18,600 households within a district that contains 74,400 households in total. What percentage of the district's households falls inside this functional region?
questions.explanation: 18,600 over 74,400 is exactly one quarter, so a quarter of the district's households lie in the catchment. The other three quarters sit outside the functional region, however close to its edge.
questions.hint: Divide the covered households by the total.

options.misconception: treats a name in a record as proof of an official boundary

options.text: The area is a vernacular region in practice, because its boundaries are drawn by how residents name it
The area has no region at all, because three different names are used for the same place
options.misconception: reads the existence of several names as the absence of any region

options.text: The area is a functional region, because patients travel from the whole district to reach the clinic
options.misconception: assumes movement to a clinic alone defines the region

questions.explanation: Several overlapping local names, used by the people who live there, make an area vernacular rather than formal. The records capture usage rather than boundaries, so they confirm but do not draw the region.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the name.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise what belongs to a site description
questions.stem: A clinic's site note lists three candidates: one on level ground with poor road access, one on a steep slope with good access, and one on flat land close to a main road. What does the note tell you about site?

options.misconception: ignores the physical constraints of the slope entirely

options.text: That the site with good road access is chosen, because access matters and the land is level
options.misconception: picks a single criterion and assumes it settles the choice

options.text: That flat ground is always the decisive factor, because building on a slope should be avoided
options.misconception: treats one physical attribute as always decisive

options.text: That each candidate has a different site, since site is the exact position and its physical attributes

questions.explanation: Site is the exact position, valued for physical attributes such as slope, level ground, and access, and each plot offers a different combination. Choosing between them is a separate judgement.

Being at the centre of the region, because the centre is the physical position of the building

options.misconception: treats a route passing the site as the site itself

options.text: Being in a valley, because a valley is a physical setting that surrounds the building
options.misconception: calls the surrounding landform the position of the building

questions.topic: Distance at which two bid-rent curves meet
questions.learningObjective: Calculate where two bid-rent curves meet
questions.stem: A site's maximum rent for a high street practice is 90 units per square metre in the centre, falling by 10 units for every 100 metres away. A warehouse will pay 60 units in the centre, falling by 5 units for every 100 metres. At what distance from the centre do the two bid-rent curves meet?

options.text: 100 metres, because the two curves close quickly where the practice's rent falls steeply
options.misconception: understates the distance by ignoring the slower decline

options.text: 900 metres, because the 30-unit gap divided by 5 units gives six steps
options.misconception: divides the gap by the wrong slope when closing the two rents

options.text: 600 metres, because the 30-unit gap closes at 5 units for every 100 metres
1,800 metres, because the practice's fall of 10 units per 100 metres sets the distance
options.misconception: uses one curve's rate of fall instead of the difference between them

questions.explanation: Equating the rents, the 30-unit gap closes at 5 units for every 100 metres, which is 6 steps or 600 metres. At that point both would pay 30 units, and beyond it the flatter warehouse curve is higher.
questions.hint: Set the two rents equal and solve for distance.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Weaken a rule-based explanation of spacing
questions.stem: A clinic's note argues that a regional chain of testing laboratories opened branches at even intervals along a corridor because of a rule in the contract. Explain why that explanation is weaker than an economic one.

answer.exemplar: A contractual spacing rule would produce a regular pattern only while it was obeyed, and it would leave the chain paying for unprofitable sites near one another. An economic account is stronger because it explains both the spacing and the places where the pattern breaks. Each laboratory needs a threshold of demand within a maximum travel range, and two outlets close together divide the same pool of patients. Where demand is weaker or a route bends, the spacing widens or the chain skips a site, which is a pattern a fixed rule cannot produce.

questions.explanation: A spacing rule explains regularity but not where it stops, and it can leave outlets trading on top of each other. Demand for a threshold population within a maximum range explains both intervals and exceptions.
questions.hint: Ask what a fixed rule cannot predict.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Distance at which two bid-rent curves meet
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a crossing decides who occupies a site
questions.stem: A clinic's site note compares a high street practice with a business park on the ring road. Explain how the point at which the two bid-rent curves cross decides which activity occupies the site.

answer.exemplar: Each curve records the highest rent one activity would pay for a location at each distance from the centre, so the higher curve wins where it lies above the other. The practice's curve starts high because it needs passing trade but falls steeply as customers become harder to attract. The business park's curve starts lower and falls gently because its advantage is space and access to roads. Where the two cross, the ordering reverses, and from that point outward the business park outbids the practice for the same plot.

questions.explanation: The activity whose curve lies higher at a given distance is the one that can outbid the other for that plot. When the curves cross, the ordering reverses, and from that distance onward the flatter curve wins.
questions.hint: Ask which curve is higher at that distance.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the maximum number of outlets
questions.stem: A region's population is 240,000. A laboratory chain needs about 15,000 people within reach of each branch to trade sustainably. At most how many branches could that chain support across the region?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risk of using vernacular names officially
questions.stem: A health board's note warns that community leaflets describing a district by its old parish name produce complaints from newer residents. Explain the problem this creates for using vernacular regions in official work.

answer.exemplar: Vernacular names are built from local history and inherited usage, and they often cover ground that does not match any administrative unit. A leaflet that calls the district by an old parish name therefore addresses people who recognise it and excludes others who do not, which is exactly the fault line visible in the complaints. Because a vernacular region has no fixed boundary, its name cannot be mapped reliably onto the population it appears to refer to, and publishing it in official material risks excluding the very households a service is meant to reach.

questions.explanation: Vernacular names carry local history and cover uneven ground, so a name that welcomes one group can exclude another. Using them officially is risky because the label cannot be mapped onto fixed households.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Advise on publishing two kinds of region
questions.stem: A health board wants to publish one map showing both its administrative districts and the areas its services actually reach. Explain why a single map cannot carry both kinds of region and what should be published instead.

answer.exemplar: Administrative districts are formal regions with boundaries set by a rule and stable over time, whereas service areas are functional regions whose edges follow the movement of patients and shift whenever a clinic opens, closes, or is reconfigured. Drawing one boundary on one map would force the two to share an edge they do not have, and it would suggest that a district's population is served by the facilities inside it, which is exactly what the functional areas disprove. The board should publish the two separately, with the date and the rule behind each, so that a reader can see where the services and the administration disagree.

questions.explanation: Formal boundaries are fixed by rule while functional edges follow where people travel, and the two rarely coincide. Publishing them separately, each dated and explained, stops readers assuming a district's facilities serve it.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Distance at which two bid-rent curves meet
questions.learningObjective: Explain why rent curves differ between uses
questions.stem: A clinician's note asks why the value of a plot for one business is greater than the value of the same plot for another. Which statement about bid-rent curves explains this?

options.text: Each activity has its own curve, and the two curves must be identical because the plot is the same
options.misconception: assumes the same plot forces identical rent curves

options.text: The two curves differ only in their starting points, because distance does not change what a plot is worth
options.misconception: believes only the intercept differs, ignoring how rent falls with distance

options.text: The curves cross at every distance, so neither activity can be said to outbid the other
options.misconception: believes smooth curves must cross repeatedly

options.text: Each activity has its own rent curve, and at this distance one curve lies above the other

questions.explanation: Each activity values a location differently, so each has its own curve of maximum rent, and both slope downward with distance. Where one lies above the other, that activity can outbid the other.
questions.hint: Ask which curve sits higher at that distance.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate planned outlet numbers
questions.stem: A region's chain of testing centres opened one branch for every 30,000 residents, and there were 240,000 residents when the plan was made. How many branches did the plan provide for, and what does that imply?

options.text: 3 branches, because only a third of the residents needed testing and the rest were served elsewhere
options.misconception: invents a service rate that the plan never stated

options.text: 8 branches, and their spacing means each covers about 30,000 people without overlapping the others
240 branches, because each of the 240,000 residents needed a branch of their own
options.misconception: treats one branch per resident as though the population were a count of outlets

options.text: 12 branches, because the population figure should be divided by the interval in kilometres
options.misconception: divides by a distance instead of by the population per branch

questions.explanation: 240,000 divided by 30,000 per branch gives 8 branches, each covering its own pool of 30,000 people. Placing them apart keeps the pools separate, which is the point of spacing them out.
questions.hint: Divide the population by the number served per branch.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes districts formal
questions.stem: A health board's note explains that its districts are drawn along parish boundaries while the population data used to describe them comes from the national count. Explain what makes the districts formal regions and what the note does not establish.

answer.exemplar: A district bounded by parish lines is a formal region because the boundary is set by a stated rule that can be applied to any place, and the same rule could be applied to the parish alone or to a much larger grouping. The note does not establish that the districts are useful for every purpose, because a formal boundary says nothing about how people travel or which services they use. A district might contain a hospital that serves people well outside its own edge, so the board's regions and its service areas need not coincide.

questions.explanation: Parish lines are a rule applied consistently, which makes the districts formal regions. The note does not establish that the boundaries match how people use services, and formal edges often cut across functional ones.
questions.hint: Ask whether a rule could draw the boundary anywhere.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Derive a total population from a service area share
questions.stem: A district hospital's functional region covers 84,000 people, which is 35 per cent of the district's total population. What is the district's total population?
questions.explanation: 84,000 divided by 0.35 gives 240,000 people in the district, of which the hospital's functional region takes just over a third. The rest is outside the service area but inside the district.
questions.hint: Divide the covered population by the percentage.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Recognise vernacular names in a community note

stimulus.body: A community nurse's note records that residents of one cluster of streets call their area the old quarter, while residents of the new housing estate across the road call the same district the town end. Neither name appears in any official record, and the boundary between the two described areas shifts with the ward boundary.

questions.stem: Using the community note, which statement about these names is best supported?

options.text: They are vernacular names, drawn from local usage and covering ground that no official boundary matches
They are formal names, because residents use them consistently in their own records
options.misconception: treats consistency of use as proof of official status

options.text: They are functional names, because both groups use the same hospital and the same schools
options.misconception: links the names to shared services that the note does not mention

options.text: They are site names, because each one marks a fixed location on the ground
options.misconception: treats a district label as a precise physical point

questions.explanation: Names residents invent, use among themselves, and apply to overlapping ground are vernacular, and the shifting edge shows they are not administrative. Nothing links them to a service or a precise point.
questions.hint: Ask who made the name up.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Apply the meaning of site to two proposals
questions.stem: A clinic's board compares two sites for a new ward. First identify what site describes, then choose the correct reading of the two proposals.

options.text: Site is the wider setting, so the proposal on the busy road has the better site
options.misconception: defines site as the wider setting and chooses wrongly

options.text: Site is the exact spot and its physical attributes, so both proposals share the same site
options.misconception: gives the right definition but overlooks the physical differences

options.text: Site is the exact spot and its physical attributes, so the two proposals offer different sites to weigh
Site is what residents call the area, so the proposal in the old quarter has the better site
options.misconception: mistakes a local name for the physical position of a facility

questions.explanation: Site is the exact spot and the physical character of the ground there, so two proposals in the same town still offer different sites to weigh. The wider setting and local naming are other descriptions.
questions.hint: Ask what each plot is physically like.
